items.content:
RT @MalwareTechBlog: I love that people want to assume that I formed my opinions on the viability of current generation open-weight LLMs for enabling low-skilled criminals to find useful zero-day exploits, based on having just never used an LLM at all. 

The first thing I did when Anthropic added me to their CVP was build an autonomous zero-day exploitation pipeline. I've since backported it to use open-weight models because the token cost was insane, so I have a fairly good feel for both current frontier and open-weight model capabilities.

I'm well aware of what LLMs are capable of doing, and that they can, with the right steering or harness find zero-day exploits. Where we drift off course is with the claim that low-skilled criminals can just pick up something like GLM and find viable zero-day exploits.

I think that: 

a) More than 90% of CVEs are functionally useless for threat actors. Threat actors have a very specific operational needs and "random issue in random software" does not fall into their scope. 

b) Many (quite possibly even the majority of) critical rated CVEs are not exploitable under real-world conditions in a way that is useful to threat actors. There's entire teams in China dedicated to n-day exploitation and watching them will give you a good feel for what percent of critical RCEs are actually useful.

c) Threat actor with no exploit development background and minimal technical skills, even with access to a completely unrestricted open-weight LLMs, would struggle or completely fail to find useful zero-day exploits.

d) People with very little experience in software exploitation, Large Language Models, and CTI, are watching professional vulnerability researchers working with next-gen frontier models and ending up with a wildly unrealistic beliefs of just how "easy" what they are doing is.

e) There is an extremely noticeable lack of both zero-day exploitation and use of novel (non-public) n-day exploits by all threat actors, especially unskilled ones, and proponents of the "anyone can just pick up GLM and find useful zero-day exploits" theory continually refuse to even acknowledge that fact, let alone attempt to explain it.

I'm not coming at this from the position of some dude who just logs on to social media to says uninformed shit. I'm coming at this from the perspective of a researcher who has spent thousands of hours since LLMs came out researching their capabilities, and has also spent their entire career tracking threat actors and their capabilities. 

I have a mountain of real-world data, because the low-skilled AI-powered threat actors have a high tendency to accidentally infect themselves with their own malware. This often results in them exfiltrate their entire hard disk, along with all their AI prompt logs, to a vibe-coded C2 with client-side authentication (the admin credentials are hardcoded into the javascript or something equally stupid, so anyone can log in and download it).

My entire career I've been very pro "degrees and certs don't matter, everyone is welcome, and the best way to gain experience is hands-on practical work". But when I have some dude whose only experience is essentially just "downloaded abliterated GLM and scared himself with it", I feel like it's necessary to draw a line somewhere.

It's not just the bad opinions, everyone has bad opinions on something, I have plenty. It's that resources are actively being diverted away from addressing real and pressing issues in cybersecurity, as a result of FUD being spread about imaginary GLM-powered zero-day wielding scriptkiddies.

items.content:
In my own head, I have a sort of visual-spacial representation how how the various system internals of iOS work 

Many other vulnerability researchers have said that their minds work similarly to reason about systems

So what I did was try to create 3D representations to map functions across all the different software/firmware/hardware layers of abstraction that these subsystems work (in this case, iOS 27's SPTM). One of the 3D representations even presents an immersive 'video game' of sorts, which lets the agents "walk through" the system 

I have found this to be a helpful resource for agents, keeping them more tightly grounded to the functionality of these complex systems, though I don't have formal benchmarks (which are overrated anyway)

items.content:
RT @HackingLZ: All the offense vs. defense stuff gets framed wrong anyway. At the end of the day, what’s the attacker’s motivation? If it’s financial, which it often is, how are they going to monetize the attack?

Work backward from there. Take unnecessary services off the internet, properly segment your DMZ, put things behind Tailscale or an application proxy, and reduce the attack surface in the first place.

If they’re already inside your network, launching a swarm of agents doesn’t magically remove the constraints of their initial foothold. They’re still potentially bottlenecked by a single compromised endpoint, its privileges, and whatever network access it has. Scaling up activity also risks creating a bunch of noisy C2 channels and generating significantly more alerts.

That creates opportunities for defenders to respond quickly, or ideally contain the activity automatically with a low false positive rate. A swarm generating an insane amount of suspicious activity might actually be easier to detect than the slower, more deliberate copy and paste playbooks many attackers have traditionally relied on.

items.content:
RT @thesupermannx: China cracked recursive self-improvement 🤯

Tencent dropped 27B model that rewrites, retrains, and refines itself.. with zero human in the loop.

It’s called "Terminal-RSI" and it solves one of the biggest problems with AI.

They are incredibly lazy.

Usually, an agent will make partial progress, claim it succeeded, and completely fail the final environment verifier check. this new pipeline forces agents to actually finish the job.

here’s how it works:

they built a recursive loop with two alternating phases..

- RSR (recursive self-rewrite): the model fine-tunes itself on its own successfully rewritten trajectories

- RPR (recursive policy-refine): it then runs reinforcement learning (ppo) using a "critic" inherited directly from the previous stage to lock in those discovered behaviors

- Loop: the training sequence leapfrogs itself: Base → RSR-1 → RPR-1 → RSR-2 → RPR-2

and the numbers are insane..

they applied this to a qwen3.8-27b base model. across the four "terminal-bench" suites, the agent's average success rate jumped from 20.68% all the way to 50.58%.

on the absolute hardest benchmark suite (terminal-bench 4.0), the base model scored a flat 0.00%.

after terminal-rsi?

it hit 19.84% (putting it right on par with reference models like gemini 3.8 flash).

the secret sauce? they fixed the reward system.

instead of giving the ai "dense rewards" for just trying or passing semantic checks, they switched to a "success-prioritized reward" (spr).

it mathematically separates strict success from partial credit.

basically, the agent only gets the massive reward payout if the code actually passes the final terminal gate.. so it stops faking success.

the gap between partial local repairs and strict terminal verification is closing fast.

we are watching agents build their own training environments and level up autonomously.. the future is wild.

items.content:
RT @sysxplore: France's cybersecurity agency just posted a fix for a hole in Linux TCP authentication, and every 32-bit kernel built with MD5 signing is exposed.

TCP-MD5 (RFC 2385) is the old signature scheme that protects BGP sessions between routers. Its successor is TCP-AO.

Jérémy Jean of ANSSI posted the v2 fix to netdev on Saturday. With TCP_MD5SIG=y and TCP_AO=n, a packet carrying a junk AO option hits a stub that returns success, so a socket requiring MD5 accepts unauthenticated data. The reverse config has the same bug.

Eric Dumazet's review was blunt: an attacker able to hit the window of an MD5-protected session "can therefore inject RST or data with a junk AO option, which is exactly what RFC 2385 is supposed to prevent."

TCP-AO depends on 64BIT, so "every 32-bit kernel with TCP_MD5SIG=y is in the vulnerable configuration." The fix is tagged for stable, reviewed by Dumazet and Kuniyuki Iwashima.

items.content:
RT @0xAsm0d3us: some alpha drop for doing inexpensive vuln research. 

instead of writing an article on the prompts/process behind this bounty (and more), I am dropping some prompts and the thought process I used as part of this research.

ik you might say prompts don't matter much, frontier models' baseline intelligence can rawdog vuln discovery (and it is true to a good extent), but there is a high chance that you either do not have access to cyber models, or even if you do, they are expensive (and with heavy guardrails). The idea is, these prompts work well with open-weight/less expensive models. Not saying these will outperform the raw intelligence and capabilities of frontier models, but open-weight models perform much better with a bounded/goal-specific approach (where the goal is set, and the search space is massive) rather than open-ended exploration (where the goal is vague, and the search space is massive).

anyway, here are some prompts. I don't need to share much, because you can just create variations of these and apply them wherever you wish.

- find places where the app is supposed to enforce something, but doesn't actually enforce it.

- find security rules that are enforced in one part of the app, but just assumed to be true in another.

- find security assumptions the app relies on, but never actually checks or enforces.

- find places where the app depends on undocumented behavior, and what happens if that behavior changes.

- find operations that are secure on their own, but become vulnerable when you combine or chain them together.

- find cases where the same object can be accessed in different ways, but each way ends up having different permissions.

- find objects whose identity can be changed or rebound to another user, without going through the right checks.

- find requests that get rejected or fail, but still end up changing something or triggering a side effect.

- find security checks that only work if certain events happen in a specific order, and what happens if that order changes.

- find operations where the transaction fails or rolls back, but some of the side effects still happen.

- find things you can still do with an object even after it has been deleted, or access to it has been revoked.

- find state changes that can be reversed or undone by someone who shouldn't have permission to do so.

- find objects that can end up in two contradictory states at the same time, and what operations become possible because of that.

I take such prompts, put it in a mutator (which has threat model of the project I am doing sec engagement), the mutator will mutate the prompts based on the threat model, and spawn swarm of agents, with different starting prompt and a bounded goal, the process repeats till all paths are exhauted, or some new signal is generated, which then feeds back to mutator. 

Doing this using a cheap model is very effective and sometimes it might yield you something even expensive models miss, we are just trying to maxximise the search space, from as many angles as possible, and once this process generates enough signals, just use a frontier model to confirm/triage issues, or for finding similar variants of such issues, that's basically it. There is v less moat is making a custom harness (unless you are an elite vuln research who can codify their approach in it or a 100x agentic engineer, I am neither).

items.content:
RT @thedealdirector: OpenAI and Anthropic have a tabula rasa problem with cybersecurity.

It’s been barely six months since the frontier labs started investing heavily in security data for model training. Once Mythos landed, it was clear the “AI breaks the game” moment had arrived.

Anthropic claimed to be very focused on working with the cybersecurity ecosystem to “integrate the model safely”, but in reality it ignored almost every conventional approach in the industry.

The biggest problem is the very one-dimensional narrative the frontier labs are building, in which the technical side of AppSec is treated as the whole field of cybersecurity.

Security is first and foremost about people, process and systems. Technology plays a useful role, but the areas where we try to reduce risk are numerous and hard to tackle. Finding and fixing bugs is just one part of the game: sometimes very important, sometimes completely irrelevant.

Exploiting a zero-day in a critical system doesn’t achieve much if the attacker has no way to move laterally within the network and only limited access to relevant data. There’s a reason the majority of successful breaches come down to insider risk and stolen credentials rather than the exploitation of novel bugs.

What AI has clearly democratized is access to zero-days. They mostly used to be in the hands of a far larger group than the nation-state actors, elite ransomware crews and occasional 200 IQ obsessive loner who traditionally had them. Today, they’re available to anyone who can spin up an abliterated LLM.

What it has really exposed is how poorly almost every company manages risk across people, process and systems. Rather than working with the wider security community to reshape how we work, the frontier labs have often chosen to be adversarial with key researchers and practitioners in the field.

To some extent, their goal is to replace every security vendor. That can look greedy, but it’s arguably well deserved. Compared with most other software categories, security vendors are far more likely to:

- Sell you software that doesn’t work at all
- Sell you software that works but breaks when integrated with the rest of your tools, making it useless
- Sell you software that works and fits into your workflow but comes with predatory pricing and deliberate lock-in

It’s one of the griftiest corners of the software industry, and the majority of practitioners hate almost every vendor with a passion. Those vendors have responded by pouring money into distribution, building large sales organizations that burn a lot of cash for very little in return.

So the frontier labs looked at this and decided to create a new problem, become the main solution to it, and then take over more and more of the industry’s technology layer over time.

Pretending that everything after Mythos is a blank slate, and that we’re only now “discovering” cybersecurity, is cynical at best and highly irresponsible at worst.

My message is simple: this strategy will fail unless you structurally focus on people and process first. Whether the leadership at OpenAI and Anthropic cares is another matter. They’ve shown repeatedly that they don’t care about the opinions of players in the ecosystem unless they’re big API consumers. 

But don’t try to erase 30 years of ideas, practices and technology just because they get in the way of token consumption.
